prompt: Noor has {m:1600} and picks an art set for {m:1000}. Which other plan now has to wait?

options.feedback: Yes. After the art set Noor has {m:600}, and the ticket costs {m:800}.
Not quite. After the art set Noor has {m:600}, so the book still fits.
Not quite. After the art set Noor has {m:600}, so lunch still fits.

hints: Work out what's left after the art set.
{m:600} is left. Which of these costs more than that?
correct: Nice. That's it. The concert waits. That's part of what the art set really cost.

prompt: Remi buys a {m:400} magazine every week instead of saving that money. How much saving is that over 5 weeks?

misconceptions.feedback: Not quite. That's one week. The same choice happens every week for 5 weeks.
Not quite. That's 4 weeks. Count all 5.

wrong: Not quite. Add {m:400} once for each week.
hints: The same choice repeats every week.
{m:400} five times. Try {m:400}, {m:800}, {m:1200} and keep going.
correct: That's it. {m:2000} over 5 weeks. It's Remi's choice, and now it's one Remi can see clearly.

prompt: Lee saves {m:400} a week. Lee spends a {m:1200} gift on a day out instead of saving it. How much later is the goal?

options.feedback: Not quite. That gift could have gone into Save. Not saving it means the goal comes later.
Not quite. Each week adds {m:400}. How many weeks make {m:1200}?

outcome: {m:1200} is 3 weeks of saving at {m:400}. Choosing the day out means the goal comes 3 weeks later. Both are fair choices, and now Lee knows the trade.
hints: How many weeks of {m:400} make {m:1200}?
{m:400}, {m:800}, {m:1200}. Count the weeks.
correct: Right. The day out costs 3 weeks of goal progress.

prompt: Why is the real cost of a choice more than just its price?

options.text: You also give up the next best thing you could have had
Prices go up after you buy
options.feedback: Not quite. The price stays the same. Think about what else the money could have done.

options.text: Every choice comes with extra fees
options.feedback: Not quite. There's no fee. The extra cost is the thing you didn't pick.

hints: Think about what else the money could have done.
If you pick the game, you can't also have the day out.
correct: Right. The real cost includes what you didn't pick.

prompt: Ari has {m:1000} and picks a hoodie for {m:650}. Could Ari still get each one on its own?
wrong: Not quite. Work out what's left after the hoodie, then compare each price.
hints: Start with what's left after the hoodie.
{m:350} is left. A price of exactly {m:350} still fits.
correct: All sorted. Anything up to {m:350} still fits. The rest is what the hoodie cost Ari.

prompt: Noor is sorting this month's list. Is each one a need or a want?

items.text: Gloves for a freezing walk to school
A ruler the teacher said to bring

wrong: Not quite. Ask: what happens without it? If Noor would be fine, it's a want.
hints: Needs are things you have to have. Wants are nice extras.
Would Noor be cold, or stuck in class, without it? Then it's a need.
correct: All sorted. Needs first, then the wants Noor chooses.

prompt: Kai has {m:900}. Kai needs {m:500} for a club trip and wants a game for {m:600}. What can Kai cover?

options.feedback: Yes. The need is covered first, and {m:400} is left.

options.text: Both the trip and the game
options.feedback: Not quite. Together they cost {m:1100}, which is more than {m:900}.
Not quite. The game fits, but then the trip doesn't. Needs come first.

hints: Cover the need first.
{m:900} take away the trip. Is the game still possible?
correct: Nice. That's it. The trip is covered and {m:400} is left. The game can wait.

prompt: Sam has {m:2500}. This week's needs are lunch money of {m:750} and a bus pass for {m:450}. How much is left for wants?

misconceptions.feedback: Not quite. That only takes off the lunch money. The bus pass is a need too.
Not quite. That only takes off the bus pass. The lunch money is a need too.
Not quite. That's what the needs cost. Take it away from {m:2500}.

wrong: Not quite. Add up the needs, then take them away from {m:2500}.
hints: Add up the needs first.
The needs come to {m:1200}. Take that away from {m:2500}.
correct: That's it. With both needs covered, {m:1300} is left for wants.

prompt: Ari's friend says headphones are a need. Ari says they're a want. How can both be right?

options.text: It depends on what each person uses them for
Needs and wants are the same thing
options.feedback: Not quite. They're different. But the same thing can be a need for one person and a want for another.
Not quite. The price doesn't decide it. What the thing is for does.

hints: Think about how each of them might use headphones.
For a music class they might be a need. Just for fun, a want.
correct: Right. The same thing can be a need for one person and a want for another.

prompt: Which of these is a want?

options.text: Sports shoes for school, as yours don't fit
options.feedback: Not quite. You need shoes that fit for sport at school. That makes them a need.
Yes. It would be fun, but you could manage without it.
Not quite. You need to eat at school. That makes it a need.

hints: A want is nice to have, but you'd manage without it.
Which one could you skip and still be fine?
correct: Nice. That's it. The concert would be fun, but you'd manage without it.
